title: Heywood cases and inadmissible solutions
summary: A negative variance estimate makes a CB-SEM solution inadmissible; it signals sampling problems, misspecification or weak identification and must be investigated, not hidden.

body.text: A [[heywood-case]] is an estimate of a variance below zero, typically a unique variance, which makes the standardised loading exceed 1. The solution is inadmissible: no real population has negative variances. Causes include sampling fluctuation with small N or a near-zero true variance, misspecification, outliers and empirical underidentification (Kolenikov & Bollen 2012).

body.explanation: For one factor with three standardised indicators (just identified), the squared loading of item 1 follows from the three correlations. With r₁₂ = r₁₃ = .85 and r₂₃ = .50 it is 1.445, so the unique variance of item 1 is 1 − 1.445 = −.445.

body.text: The starter reproduces exactly that case. SEM Lab flags the solution as inadmissible, names the indicator and also notes that the model is just identified (df = 0), so its "perfect" fit carries no information.

Investigate the data and the specification; test whether the negative estimate is compatible with a small positive variance (if its confidence interval includes zero, sampling error is a plausible cause; Kolenikov & Bollen 2012); consider more indicators or a theoretically better model. Fixing the variance to zero or a small positive value is a constraint that must be justified and reported.

mistake.title: Fixing the variance at .001 and reporting the fit
mistake.text: Silencing the warning with a constraint hides the symptom and leaves its cause. If you impose a constraint, report why, report the unconstrained result, and treat the fit with caution.

tryIt.task: Run CB-SEM on this three-indicator factor. Read the warnings, the negative unique variance and the standardised loading of h1.

checks.question: A standardised loading of 1.20 appears. What does it imply?

options.text: A negative unique variance: the solution is inadmissible and must be investigated.

options.feedback: Standardised loadings above 1 are impossible in a proper solution.
Rounding cannot push a loading from below 1 to 1.20.

options.text: Check data and specification, examine the interval of the negative variance, and report what you did.
Constrain the variance to .001 and report the fit indices as usual.
options.feedback: The constraint hides the problem; the fit is not interpretable as if nothing happened.

options.text: Switch to PLS-SEM to make the warning disappear.
options.feedback: Changing estimand to avoid a diagnostic does not address its cause.
